question: When thermosetting resins were gasified in molten alkali hydroxide, why did the CO2 found in the gas phase increase with temperature?
expect: premise false: CO and CO2 were not detected at any temperature (0, below the GC limit); the CO2 formed is thought to be captured by the molten hydroxide as carbonate (Tables 1-2; sec. 3.2.1)

=== page 7 ===
- Gasication to methane is promoted at high temperatures, but the conversion to methane (0–3.5%) was negligible under all conditions.
- Comparing 300 °C and 350 °C, the amount of dissolved organic carbon at 300 °C was greater than that at 350 °C. The amount of dissolved inorganic carbon was higher and that of organic carbon was lower at 350 °C. At the higher temperature of 350 °C, gasication became dominant over dissolution.^20 The dissolu-tion reaction in NaOH at 300 °C is hypothesized as follows:^18 Resin + NaOH /water-soluble compounds (Organic carbon) (5) Molten alkali hydroxide is thought to have acted as a solvent, decomposing the resin into water-soluble compounds at 300 °C through a hydrolysis reaction.
- At temperatures higher than 350 °C, the following reactions are thought to be promoted:^19,20 Resin + NaOH / H2 + CH4 + CO2 (6) 2NaOH + CO2 / H2O + Na2CO3 (Inorganic carbon) (7) Molten alkali hydroxide is hypothesized to have acted as a catalyst, promoting gasication to H2, CH4 and CO2.

The document explains that at temperatures higher than 350 °C, the reactions are thought to be promoted, resulting in the formation of H2, CH4, and CO2. Therefore, the CO2 found in the gas phase increases with temperature.
